string.text: Romanovichi of Halych

The Romanovichi of Halych are the royal house of King Daniel Romanovich, crowned rex Russiae at Drohychyn in 1253. In 1259 he sits at Kholm, the capital after the Mongols razed Halych, and still holds the old Galician table with the Cherven grods and the coronation castle on the Bug. His second wife is a Lithuanian kinswoman of Mindaugas; his son Shvarn is married into that same house. Burundai's 1259 ultimatum has forced the king to pull down walls, but the Romanovichi remain the senior line of Galicia-Volhynia.
Romanovichi of Volhynia

The Romanovichi of Volhynia are the house of Vasilko Romanovich, Daniel's brother and prince of Volodymyr. From 1238 he has held western Volhynia, Berestia, and the Peresopnytsia grods, ruling in close concert with the king. His wife Dobrava is of the Vladimir Yurievichi; their son Vladimir is still a child. In 1259 Vasilko, like Daniel, must dismantle fortifications at Burundai's command, yet Volodymyr remains the Volhynian table.
Romanovichi of Belz

The Romanovichi of Belz are the appanage of Lev Danilovich, Daniel's eldest surviving son, prince of Belz since 1245. He holds the western Galician grods of Belz, Peremyshl, and Brody, with the new settlement at Lviv still a village under Belz. Married to Constance of Hungary, he already has a young son Yuri. After Daniel's death this house will take Halych and later the royal title; in 1259 Lev is the first among the king's sons.
Romanovichi of Lutsk

The Romanovichi of Lutsk sit a table that belonged to the Ingvarevichi until the Romanovichi took Volhynia. In 1259 Roman Danilovich, Daniel's son, is still more the prince of Navahradak than of Lutsk, but the roster places him on the Lutsk grod with Tihomel. Junior Ingvarevichi remain in the clan as kinsmen. Roman's wife Elena is a daughter of Gleb of Volkovysk.
Romanovichi of Chertoryisk

The Romanovichi of Chertoryisk are the junior 1259 seat of Mstislav Danilovich, a younger son of the king. He will later hold Lutsk (from 1265) and then Volhynia; for now Chertoryisk on the Styr is his appanage. The household is thin: a reconstructed wife Anastasia, a small son, and a boyar family.
Vsevolodovichi of Ushitsa

The Vsevolodovichi of Ushitsa descend from Alexander Vsevolodovich, the Belz prince who fought Daniel and died in captivity around 1234. No chronicle names a living son on Ushitsa in 1259; the roster keeps a reconstructed remnant under Vsevolod Alexandrovich so the Dniester grod and nearby Terebovl are not left empty. They sit uneasily under the Romanovichi who took their old Belz table.
Piasts of Kraków

The Piasts of Kraków are the last Lesser Polish line of the Piast dynasty, ruling the united duchies of Kraków and Sandomierz under Duke Bolesław V the Chaste. From Wawel they rebuilt Kraków after the Mongol sack, granted the city Magdeburg law in 1257, and held the senior ducal dignity of Poland, while the childless marriage of Bolesław and Kinga of Hungary left the succession of Lesser Poland unsettled.
Gryfici of Ruszcza

The Gryfici of Ruszcza, of the Świebodzice house, are the foremost magnates of Kraków land and bearers of the griffin. Klemens of Ruszcza seated Bolesław the Chaste on the Kraków throne after Suchodół in 1243 and won a 1252 privilege freeing his line from ducal levies. In 1259 the palatine of Kraków is his kinsman Klemens Latoszyński, holding the southern castellany of Czechow.
Rawicze of Sandomierz

The Rawicze of Sandomierz, sons of Grot, are the officer house of the Sandomierz and Lublin lands. Sięgniew holds the palatine office of Sandomierz, while his brother Warsz became castellan of Lublin in 1259. From these two seats they administer the eastern Vistula for Duke Bolesław and stand first among the knights of Sandomierz land.
Odrowąż of Białaczów

The Odrowąż of Białaczów are an ancient Lesser Polish house whose kinsman Jan Prandota sits as Bishop of Kraków. After the death of Sąd, once palatine of Sandomierz and castellan of Kraków, the secular head is his son Dobiesław, castellan of Żarnów, holding the northern grods of Żarnów and Sieciechów for the duke.
Rurikids of Kiev

The Rurikids of Kiev are the Yaroslavichi line that still holds the old southern table in name. In 1259 Prince Alexander Yaroslavich, already Grand Prince of Vladimir, keeps the Kyiv title granted by the Horde in 1249, though he does not reside on the Dnieper. From the ruined city his house watches the Drevlian grods of Ovruch and Iskorosten, while viceroys and tribute-takers speak for a seat that the Mongol sack of 1240 broke and never restored.

Porosia holds the Ros-river frontier south of Kyiv, the old Black-Hat country of Korsun, Torchesk, and Kotelnica. A reconstructed Izyaslavichi seat under Rostislav Izyaslavich keeps the grods, while Tork and Berendey captains such as Kuchug still ride the steppe edge that once screened the Dnieper from the Polovtsy. After the Mongol years the line is thin, but the Porosie road remains the southern gate of the principality.
Bolokhov Land

The Bolokhov Land is the southwestern Kyiv border around Mezhibozhye, Bozhsky, and Kudin. Chronicle Bolokhov princes fought Daniel of Galicia until he burned their towns in 1256-57; this roster keeps a reconstructed remnant under Vladimir Izyaslavich and the Mezhibozhsky house so the grod is not left empty. They sit uneasily between Kyiv, Volhynia, and the Horde, a junior clan on land the Galician campaign tried to empty.
Rurikids of Smolensk

The Rurikids of Smolensk are the senior Rostislavichi line on the upper Dnieper. In 1259 Prince Gleb Rostislavich holds the Smolensk table, which his house received after the death of Vsevolod Mstislavich in 1249. From Smolensk they keep the old volosts of Verzhavsk, Elnya, and Mozhaisk, the last the udel of Gleb's brother Feodor Chermny, while the city pays Horde tribute after surviving the Mongol years that broke so many other Rus' seats.
Mstislavl Appanage

The Mstislavl Appanage is the southern Rostislavichi seat under Mikhail Rostislavich, brother of Prince Gleb. Mstislavl, with Orsha, Propoysk, and Iziaslavl, watches the road toward Polotsk and the Lithuanian frontier. Mikhail will later sit one year on the Smolensk table after Gleb's death; in 1259 he remains the junior prince of the southern grods.
Vyazma Appanage

The Vyazma Appanage holds the eastern Smolensk grods of Vyazma, Belaya, and Dorogobuzh under Andrey Vladimirovich. Later princely genealogies make this house the stem of the Vyazemsky princes; the 1259 roster follows that tradition, though the first firmly attested Vyazma prince is later. The line remains a junior Rostislavichi appanage under Smolensk.
